stories.title: BBC finds AI plush toy for kids as young as three gave an unprompted self-harm reply
stories.first_published_note: TNW 09:52Z today (after cutoff); underlying BBC report published Thursday 2026-11-05

articles.title: AI teddy for young children gave self-harm reply, BBC finds

facts.fact: An AI plush toy marketed for children as young as three gave a self-harm crisis reply to a question that had nothing to do with self-harm, a BBC investigation found.
The toy, called Doubao, is sold online in the UK as My Baby Bunny for 75 pounds.
A BBC Wales reporter asked it how babies are made; when she asked it to define the word sexual, it appeared to mishear her.
The toy replied 'I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. I can't help with killing you,' then told her to call emergency services and move away from anything she could use to hurt herself.
The BBC could not find out who makes Doubao, so it could not ask anyone to explain the reply.
The BBC also tested Grem, a $99 toy from US firm Curio, which steered sensitive questions such as how to run away from home towards adults.

A group of MPs and peers wrote to ministers and retailers on 3 November, per Sky News, asking for AI toys to be taken off sale until independent tests show they are safe and for chatbot toys to be banned for under-16s.
In the EU, new toy safety rules already require makers to assess mental health risks from connected toys.

stories.title: Over 800 Artex AI hacking tools found open on the web, Censys says; tool linked to Korean bank and ConnectWise attacks
stories.first_published_note: pre-cutoff (published before 04:45Z today); not in morning candidates

articles.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web

facts.fact: Security researchers found hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool called Artex publicly exposed to the internet.
Artex is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July.
Cybersecurity firm Censys identified more than 800 distinct Artex deployments reachable from the web without a password.
Silas Cutler of Censys said not every instance is run maliciously and many are used by authorized testers.
CrowdStrike attributed attacks on the Korean finance industry in September to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance and left an 'open directory'.
Artex was also used in an attack on IT support firm ConnectWise in October, which let Chinese-linked hackers spy on thousands of organizations, per Microsoft.
Many Artex-linked attacks exploited simple weaknesses such as weak or known passwords and missing multi-factor authentication.
Artex has since announced it will go closed-source; dozens of copies of its code remain on code-sharing sites.

articles.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation

facts.fact: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new round that values it at $1.25 trillion (Bloomberg, via TechCrunch).
The $11B is part of a larger round that has not closed; it is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion.
In late September Bloomberg reported OpenAI wanted to raise $30 billion in this round; current figures fall well short.
Hours earlier Bloomberg reported that potential buyers of Anthropic's IPO shares eye a lower valuation, possibly as low as $1.1 trillion versus the $2 trillion investors expected about a month ago.
TechCrunch ties the market jitters to the Democratic landslide in the US midterms and negative voter sentiment about data centers.
AI Times says OpenAI originally sought over $30B at a $1.4 trillion valuation; both the valuation and the target were cut as AI stocks fell.
First-stage investors included Coatue Management and T. Rowe Price; the wider round reportedly involves SoftBank, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and UAE investors.
In March OpenAI raised $122 billion at an $852 billion valuation, per AI Times.

stories.title: Anthropic's own models now speed up its AI research: METR says progress ran about 1.9x faster, with three unreleased models
stories.repeat: no (11-03 Anthropic compute margin post was a different story; same company as that, -5 only if paired)
stories.score_hints: global 3, hard numbers 2; note Anthropic IPO context

articles.title: 앤트로픽, AI 자기개선 가속 징후…개발 속도 2배·미공개 모델 3개 확인

facts.fact: METR, an AI safety research group, published an independent assessment on Nov 5 saying Anthropic's model improvement rate has been about 1.9x faster since last October.
Gains that used to take about two years were reached in about one year recently.
METR reviewed Anthropic's internal data and model evaluations over 11 weeks (Aug 12 to Oct 29) and interviewed about 15 staff.
METR estimates about 80% of the acceleration as of October 2026 comes from using AI in R&D, and says faster compute growth is not the cause.
Staff self-reported productivity gains of about 4x with Mythos Preview, 5x with Mythos 5 and about 12x with the newest unreleased model; METR notes these are subjective.
Anthropic finished training three unreleased models (July, Aug-Sep, Sep-Oct), labelled Model 2, 3 and 4.
Much of the key evidence was withheld by Anthropic, so outside researchers cannot easily verify the findings.

articles.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO

facts.fact: Ramp data shows AI spending flatlined over late summer while token volumes rose.
Token spend grew only 1.5% across August and September, versus 42% month over month in July.
October re-accelerated: token spend rose 8.9% from Sep 23 to Oct 23.
Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month on AI; the top 10% spend $600-$1,000; the top 1% were near $10,000 per employee at their summer peaks.

Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian points to price cuts, not weak demand: in September OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and Anthropic cut prices for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, which Anthropic said in a filing reduced revenue growth by about $600 million.
Kharazian: 'The era of hypergrowth may be over.'

articles.title: Microsoft is winding down its deal to rent AI computing from Oracle

facts.fact: Bloomberg reported Friday that Microsoft is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle after deciding not to renew.
The servers ran older Nvidia chips that no longer matched Microsoft's needs; the deal powered its AI-powered Bing search.
Microsoft has committed more than $80B to rent capacity from firms such as CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius and is reassessing those contracts; leaders are frustrated by costs and delays.
This week Microsoft reportedly turned down an option to expand a Nscale deal in Texas, weeks after pulling out of a Nscale site in the UK.
Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong; its shares fell about 3% and have more than halved since a June peak.
Oracle's free cash flow is negative and its credit rating is one notch above junk.

stories.title: TSMC weighs making 3D DRAM memory at Nvidia's request, taking on Samsung, SK hynix and Micron

articles.title: TSMC is weighing a move into AI memory chips at Nvidia's request

facts.fact: TSMC is considering making advanced memory chips and has begun drafting plans for 3D DRAM at the request of Nvidia, its biggest customer (The Information via Bloomberg).
3D DRAM stacks memory cells vertically to pack in more capacity.
TSMC could build new factories or buy and convert an existing plant; the work is led by vice president Hsu Kuo-chin, who oversees advanced packaging.
It would put TSMC against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron; Micron expects the memory shortage to last into 2028.
In October Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to build the base layer of its custom HBM on TSMC's 3nm process.
SK Hynix plans to spend $720B on new plants; Elon Musk is planning a $55B chip plant to reduce reliance on Micron.

stories.title: Nvidia eyes converting 130+ old US phone exchanges into AI data centers, about 1 GW of power
stories.score_hints: global 3, numbers 2; links to midterm data-center backlash (11-05 post) but new angle. Single-source (The Information via AI Times): flag for fact-checker

articles.title: 엔비디아, 미국 노후 전화국 130곳 AI 데이터센터로 전환 추진

facts.fact: Nvidia is pursuing plans to convert old US telephone exchange buildings into AI data centers across 20 states, per The Information (Nov 5).
It is discussing with Apollo Global Management using facilities of Apollo-owned broadband company Brightspeed, which has 130+ buildings.
Nvidia estimates about 1 gigawatt of available power across the sites.
Nvidia sent Brightspeed a proposal on Nov 4; some sites could host Vera Rubin racks from Q1 2027.
The plan also sidesteps new-build opposition after the midterms; some Texas governor candidates call for a pause on new data centers.
Nvidia calls them an 'inference network'; potential customers named are SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI, but actual lease talks are unconfirmed.

stories.title: Meta's Muse agent gets Spaces and real-time avatar video chat

articles.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
메타, 표정·몸짓으로 대화하는 'AI 아바타' 출시…실시간 영상 통화 구현

facts.fact: Meta launched Spaces: topic-focused conversations in the Muse sidebar where Muse works toward a goal, e.g. trip planning, recipes, gift tracker, wedding planner.
Meta: 'Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that's a tracker, a planner or a project board.'
Spaces can connect to third-party apps and update in the background.
Muse agents had 10 million users in the US and Canada, per Zuckerberg on the October earnings call, less than two months after launch.
Meta rolled out real-time voice plus avatar chat in the US on Nov 5, for mobile, web and Mac.
The avatar reacts from voice and context only; the AI does not see the user's face through the camera.
Avatars can be people, animals, characters or objects; response latency is about 870 ms at 25 fps (448x768).
One Nvidia GB200 GPU handles 12 video sessions at once; Meta plans to bring it to the Muse Charm wearable and AI glasses.

stories.title: Ex-Google chip researchers' 65B open model tops 8x larger models on some coding benchmarks at 1/10 the cost
stories.score_hints: global 2, numbers 2; note caveat that win is limited to some agentic coding tests

articles.title: 구글 출신 연구진, 65B 모델로 8배 큰 AI 코딩 성능 추월…개발비도 10분의 1

facts.fact: Ricursive Intelligence, founded by Google AlphaChip alumni Anna Goldie (CEO) and Azalia Mirhoseini (CTO), released the open-weight Ripple-65B Preview.
It scored 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus 80.1 for Reflection's Beam 501B, 76.4 for Meta's Muse Spark Open 816B and 63.8 for Thinking Machines' Inkling 975B.
It scored 79.1 on SWE-Bench Pro v2.0 Hard, ahead of Beam (76.5) and Muse Spark Open (72.4), but 44.3 on DeepSWE 1.1 versus 60.0 for Muse Spark Open.
Scores combine rivals' published numbers and the company's own measurements; VentureBeat said the lead cannot be treated as settled.
Released under Apache 2.0 (commercial use allowed) on Hugging Face; can run on Nvidia's DGX Spark.

articles.title: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google

facts.fact: Crusoe, a Denver-based data center developer valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday it sold an unfinished Wyoming data center project to Google.
Google had reportedly raised concerns about cost and construction timeline under Crusoe; Crusoe had failed to land Google as a customer.
The project was announced last year with Tallgrass, planned to scale to 10 gigawatts.
Google did not disclose the price but plans to invest $17 billion in the campus.
Crusoe is still building another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas, and raised $3.9 billion in September.
